We need to find a retrosynthetic template for carbonyl-ene reaction reverse. The forward carbonyl-ene: carbonyl + alkene -> new C-C bond, alcohol, and a new C-C bond, forming a five-membered ring? Actually carbonyl-ene forms a new C-C bond between alkene carbon and carbonyl carbon, moving double bond, forming an allylic alcohol. In retrosynthesis, we need to break a C-C bond (the one formed) and form a carbonyl and an alkene. The target molecule includes a cyclopentanol fused to aromatic? Let's examine SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Interpretation: It's a bicyclic? There's a phenyl attached to an exocyclic alkene (CH2= C(aryl) - chiral center attached to cyclopentanol with CF3? Actually C15 with three Fs is CF3 attached to same carbon as the cyclopentane? The cyclopentane ring: C9 (chiral) attached to CH2-CH2-CH2- C13 (chiral) bearing OH and attached to C15(CF3). So the carbonyl-ene would have been a carbonyl (maybe a ketone) reacting with an alkene to give this product. The reverse would be to break the C-O bond (alcohol) to carbonyl, break C-C bond between C9 and C13? Actually the carbonyl-ene forms a new C-C bond between the alkene carbon (C2?) and the carbonyl carbon (C13?). In product we have a five-membered ring formed (cyclopentanol). So the precursor likely is a ketone (maybe a cyclopentanone) and an alkene (the exocyclic alkene). The carbonyl-ene would give a cyclopentanol with a new C-C bond linking the alkene carbon to the carbonyl carbon, forming a new C-C bond and moving the double bond to an allylic position, generating an allylic alcohol.

Thus retrosynthetic step: target -> break C-O bond to carbonyl (ketone) and break C-C bond to give alkene and carbonyl separate.

We need to find a template ID that matches this transformation. Use get_available_functional_groups to see valid names.
